_meta.disclaimer: This information is general educational material compiled from publicly available agricultural extension references. It is not a diagnosis. Confirm any suspected disease with a plant diagnostic laboratory or extension specialist before taking action.
_meta.sources_note: Entries were compiled from general plant-pathology knowledge as published by the land-grant university extension services and professional bodies listed under each class. URLs point to each organisation's plant-disease resource portal rather than to individual pages, because page addresses change frequently. Chemical control is deliberately not prescribed; consult local, current recommendations and product labels.

Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is the most common fungal disease of apple in cool, moist growing regions. It attacks leaves, fruit and sometimes twigs, and heavy infections cause early leaf drop and unmarketable fruit.
symptoms: Olive-green to dark brown spots with a velvety, feathery margin on leaves, usually on the upper surface first
Spots darken and may merge; infected leaves can curl, yellow and fall prematurely
On fruit: rough, corky, dark 'scab' lesions that may crack as the fruit grows
environmental_factors: Cool, wet spring weather with extended leaf wetness during bud break and early leaf growth
Spores are released from fallen, infected leaves of the previous season during rain
Dense, poorly ventilated canopies dry slowly and favour infection
prevention: Plant scab-resistant cultivars where available
Rake up and destroy (or shred and compost thoroughly) fallen leaves in autumn to reduce overwintering inoculum
Prune to open the canopy and speed leaf drying; avoid overhead irrigation
Protective fungicide programmes exist and are timed from green tip; follow local extension guidance and product labels
next_steps: Compare lesions on several leaves and on fruit; scab is often confirmed by the combination
Contact your local extension service or a diagnostic lab to confirm and to obtain a locally appropriate management schedule
Record first appearance dates to improve timing next season

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot affects apple leaves (as 'frogeye leaf spot'), fruit (black rot) and branches (cankers). The fungus survives in dead wood, cankers and mummified fruit.
symptoms: Leaves: small purple specks that enlarge into roughly circular brown spots with a purple margin, often with a lighter 'frog-eye' centre
Fruit: brown to black rot, frequently starting at the calyx end, with concentric dark rings; fruit may shrivel into mummies
Branches: sunken, cracked cankers on limbs, often on wood weakened by fire blight or winter injury
environmental_factors: Warm, wet weather during the growing season
Infection usually enters through wounds, pruning cuts or stressed tissue
Dead wood, old cankers and mummified fruit left in the orchard provide spores
prevention: Remove and destroy dead wood, cankered limbs and mummified fruit; prune out fire-blight-killed tissue
Maintain tree vigour and avoid wounding bark
Fungicides used for scab provide partial protection; consult local recommendations
next_steps: Inspect limbs for cankers and the orchard floor for mummified fruit
Confirm with an extension specialist; leaf symptoms can resemble other leaf spots

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar-apple rust needs two hosts: it overwinters as galls on junipers (eastern red cedar) and infects apple leaves and fruit in spring. It cannot spread from apple to apple.
symptoms: Bright yellow to orange spots on the upper leaf surface, often with a reddish border
Tiny black dots (spermogonia) form in the spots; later, small tube-like structures appear on the leaf underside
Severe infection causes leaf yellowing and drop; fruit can show similar orange lesions
environmental_factors: Spring rains trigger spore release from orange, gelatinous galls on nearby junipers
Spores travel hundreds of metres or more on the wind
Wet leaves for several hours at moderate temperatures favour infection
prevention: Plant resistant apple cultivars
Remove nearby junipers/red cedars where practical, or remove galls from them before spring
Protective fungicides timed from pink bud through the early cover sprays are used in commercial orchards; follow local guidance
next_steps: Look for galls on junipers within a few hundred metres
Confirm with your extension service, especially before any fungicide decisions

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew produces a white, powdery fungal growth on cherry leaves, shoots and sometimes fruit. Young, actively growing tissue is most susceptible.
symptoms: White to grey powdery patches on leaves, often starting on the undersides or on young terminal leaves
Infected leaves may curl, pucker or become distorted
On fruit: circular whitish patches, later rough or russeted areas
environmental_factors: Warm days and cool nights with high humidity; unlike many fungi it does not need free water on the leaf
Shaded, dense canopies and vigorous succulent growth increase susceptibility
The fungus overwinters in buds and on fallen leaves
prevention: Prune for light penetration and airflow
Avoid excessive nitrogen that promotes soft growth
Manage irrigation so leaves do not stay humid; drip irrigation is preferable
Sulfur and other protectant products are commonly used in orchards; consult local extension guidance and labels
next_steps: Check young terminal leaves and fruit for powdery growth
Confirm with an extension service if the orchard is commercial or the disease is spreading

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Gray leaf spot is a residue-borne fungal disease that can cause significant yield loss when it reaches the upper leaves before grain fill.
symptoms: Small tan spots that elongate into narrow, rectangular grey to tan lesions bounded by the leaf veins
Lesions may be 1-6 cm long and can merge to blight whole leaves
Starts on the lower leaves and moves upward
environmental_factors: Warm temperatures with high humidity and long periods of leaf wetness or dew
Continuous corn and reduced tillage leave infected residue on the soil surface
Low-lying fields with poor air movement
prevention: Choose hybrids with good gray leaf spot resistance ratings
Rotate away from corn and manage residue to reduce inoculum
Fungicide applications are sometimes economic around tasselling in high-risk fields; use regional scouting thresholds
next_steps: Scout lower leaves before tasselling and note the proportion of leaf area affected
Consult extension or an agronomist about thresholds for your hybrid and growth stage

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Common rust appears on corn leaves as rusty pustules. It rarely causes economic loss in field corn but can be important in sweet corn and seed production.
symptoms: Small, oval to elongated cinnamon-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces that rupture the leaf skin
Pustules turn dark brown to black late in the season
Severe cases produce yellowing and premature leaf death
environmental_factors: Cool to moderate temperatures (roughly 16-25 °C) with high humidity and dew
Spores are carried long distances by wind from regions where the fungus survives year-round
Does not overwinter in cold climates on residue
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids, particularly for sweet corn
Scout early; fungicide is usually only justified in sweet corn or seed fields with early, heavy infection
Avoid late plantings in regions where rust arrives late in the season
next_steps: Distinguish from southern rust, which has smaller, lighter pustules mostly on the upper surface and is more damaging
Ask an extension agronomist whether treatment is warranted for your crop type

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern leaf blight produces long, cigar-shaped lesions. Yield loss is greatest when the disease develops on upper leaves before or during silking.
symptoms: Long (2-15 cm), elliptical or 'cigar-shaped' grey-green to tan lesions not limited by leaf veins
Lesions may show dark sporulation in humid weather and can merge to kill large leaf areas
Usually begins on lower leaves
environmental_factors: Moderate temperatures (about 18-27 °C) and extended leaf wetness from dew, rain or fog
Residue from previous corn crops is the primary inoculum source
Continuous corn and minimum tillage increase risk
prevention: Select hybrids with resistance (including Ht resistance genes effective against local races)
Rotate crops and manage residue
Foliar fungicides may be used in high-risk fields near tasselling; follow regional recommendations
next_steps: Scout from about V8 onward, especially in fields with corn residue
Confirm with extension; lesions can be confused with other leaf blights

Grape___Black_rot.description: Black rot is one of the most damaging grape diseases in warm, humid regions. Leaf spots are the early sign; fruit infection destroys the crop by turning berries into hard black mummies.
symptoms: Small, roughly circular tan to reddish-brown leaf spots with a darker margin
Tiny black dots (pycnidia) develop inside the leaf spots, often in a ring
Berries develop a light spot, then rot, shrivel and harden into black 'mummies' that stay attached to the cluster
environmental_factors: Warm, wet weather; infection needs leaf wetness for several hours
Mummified berries left on the vine or the ground release spores in spring
Dense canopies that dry slowly
prevention: Remove mummies and infected canes during dormant pruning; drop them away from the vineyard
Manage the canopy (shoot positioning, leaf removal) for air movement
Fungicide programmes from early shoot growth to a few weeks after bloom are used commercially; follow local guidance
next_steps: Check clusters for shrivelled, black berries
Consult an extension viticulture specialist for a locally timed programme

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).scientific_name: Complex of fungi incl. Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium spp. and Fomitiporia spp.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: Esca is a grapevine trunk disease complex. Fungi colonise the wood through pruning wounds; foliar symptoms appear years later and can vary from season to season.
symptoms: Interveinal yellowing (white cultivars) or reddening (red cultivars) that dries to form 'tiger-stripe' patterns between the veins
Dark spots or speckling on berries ('measles')
Sudden wilting and collapse of all or part of a vine in hot weather ('apoplexy')
environmental_factors: Infection occurs mainly through fresh pruning wounds during wet weather
Older vines and vines with large pruning cuts are more affected
Symptoms are often worse in hot, dry summers following wet springs
prevention: Prune late in the dormant season and in dry weather; protect large wounds with registered wound protectants where available
Remove and destroy dead wood and severely affected vines
Use clean nursery stock and avoid unnecessary large cuts
next_steps: Cut into the trunk of a declining vine to look for dark streaking or soft, spongy wood (a specialist can help)
There is no curative treatment once the wood is infected; discuss remedial surgery or replacement with an extension viticulturist

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: A late-season fungal leaf spot of grape. It is less studied than black rot or downy mildew, and published management guidance is limited.
symptoms: Irregular to angular dark brown to black spots on the leaf, often with a lighter centre as they age
A greyish fungal growth may be visible on the lower surface of spots in humid weather
Severe infections cause yellowing and early leaf drop late in the season
environmental_factors: Warm, humid conditions late in the growing season
Dense canopies and poor air movement
The fungus survives on fallen leaves
prevention: Canopy management to improve airflow and spray coverage
Remove and destroy fallen leaves
Fungicides applied for other grape diseases may give incidental control; specific recommendations are limited—ask local extension
next_steps: Rule out downy mildew (which shows white, fluffy growth on the underside) and black rot
Submit a sample to a diagnostic laboratory for confirmation; information on this disease is less complete than for others

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).scientific_name: 'Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus' (also Ca. L. americanus, Ca. L. africanus)
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).pathogen_type: bacterium (phloem-limited), spread by the Asian citrus psyllid
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: HLB is the most serious citrus disease worldwide. The bacterium is spread by psyllid insects and by grafting infected budwood. There is no cure; infected trees decline and produce unusable fruit.
symptoms: Blotchy, asymmetrical yellow mottling of leaves (unlike nutrient deficiencies, which are usually symmetrical across the midrib)
Yellow shoots scattered through the canopy; thickened, upright leaves with corky veins
Small, lopsided fruit that stay partly green, with bitter juice and aborted seeds; twig dieback and tree decline
environmental_factors: Presence of the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri) or the African psyllid
Movement of infected plants or budwood
Warm climates where psyllid populations are high year-round
prevention: Buy only certified, disease-free nursery trees
Monitor and manage psyllids; follow regional area-wide programmes
Remove confirmed infected trees promptly to protect neighbours
Do not move citrus plant material out of quarantine areas
next_steps: HLB is a regulated (quarantine) disease in many countries and regions: report suspected trees to your plant-protection authority or extension office
Laboratory (PCR) testing is required for confirmation; visual symptoms alone are not definitive

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot affects peach leaves, twigs and fruit. It is hard to control once established and is most severe in warm, wet, windy seasons and on sandy sites.
symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked leaf spots that turn purple-brown; the centres often fall out leaving a 'shot-hole' appearance
Spots concentrate near the leaf tip and margins; infected leaves yellow and drop, sometimes causing heavy defoliation
Fruit show small dark pits that can crack; twigs develop cankers
environmental_factors: Warm, wet weather with wind-driven rain spreads bacteria from twig cankers
Light, sandy soils and exposed, windy sites increase severity
Bacteria overwinter in twig cankers and leaf scars
prevention: Plant cultivars rated as less susceptible
Avoid windy, sandy sites or use windbreaks
Maintain balanced nutrition; stressed trees defoliate more readily
Copper- and antibiotic-based programmes are used in commercial orchards with strict timing and resistance concerns; follow local recommendations
next_steps: Check twigs for cankers and fruit for pitting to support the identification
Consult an extension fruit specialist; bacterial spot can be confused with fungal shot-hole

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.scientific_name: Xanthomonas euvesicatoria and related species (X. vesicatoria, X. perforans, X. gardneri)
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot is a seed- and transplant-borne disease that spreads by splashing water. It causes leaf spots, defoliation and scabby fruit lesions, and is difficult to control once established.
symptoms: Small water-soaked spots that become brown, sometimes with a yellow halo; spots may be angular and the centres may tear out
Leaves yellow and drop, exposing fruit to sunscald
Raised, rough, scabby spots on fruit
environmental_factors: Warm temperatures with rain, overhead irrigation or heavy dew
Introduced on infected seed or transplants; spread by splashing water, tools and workers handling wet plants
Survives on crop debris and volunteer plants
prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seed and healthy transplants
Rotate out of peppers and tomatoes for at least a year and remove crop debris
Avoid working with plants when wet and use drip irrigation
Resistant cultivars exist for some bacterial races; copper products are commonly used but resistance is widespread—seek local advice
next_steps: Inspect fruit for scabby spots to support the identification
Submit a sample to a diagnostic lab; several bacteria and fungi cause similar spots

Potato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is a common fungal disease that affects older leaves first. Despite its name it usually appears mid to late season, especially on stressed or senescing plants.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with concentric rings ('target' or 'bull's-eye' pattern), often surrounded by a yellow halo
Lesions begin on the lower, older leaves and progress upward
Severe infection causes leaf death and defoliation; tubers may show dark, sunken, corky lesions
environmental_factors: Warm temperatures (roughly 24-29 °C) with alternating wet and dry periods
Plants under stress from poor nutrition, drought or insect damage are more susceptible
The fungus survives in soil and crop debris
prevention: Rotate potatoes and tomatoes with unrelated crops for 2-3 years
Maintain balanced fertility and avoid water stress
Remove or bury infected debris after harvest
Protectant fungicide programmes are used commercially; consult regional forecasting guidance
next_steps: Compare with late blight: early blight lesions have concentric rings and dry edges, late blight lesions are larger and water-soaked
Consult extension if the disease is spreading up the plant before tuber bulking

Potato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is the disease behind the Irish potato famine. It can destroy a crop within days in cool, wet weather and spreads rapidly between fields, so it is treated as a community-wide problem.
symptoms: Large, irregular, pale to dark green water-soaked blotches that turn brown or black, often starting at leaf tips or edges
A white, fuzzy mould on the underside of lesions in humid conditions
Dark lesions on stems; tubers develop reddish-brown, granular rot under the skin
environmental_factors: Cool (10-25 °C), wet, humid weather with long leaf-wetness periods
Infected seed tubers, cull piles and volunteer potatoes are the main sources
Spores travel by wind and rain between fields
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers and destroy cull piles and volunteers
Choose cultivars with late blight resistance
Follow regional disease-forecasting systems and act early; protectant fungicides are the main commercial tool
Destroy infected foliage promptly and allow it to die before harvest to protect tubers
next_steps: Act quickly: confirm with your extension service or a diagnostic lab the same day
Inform neighbouring growers if confirmed; late blight spreads between farms and gardens
Remove and bag (do not compost) infected plants in home gardens

Squash___Powdery_mildew.scientific_name: Podosphaera xanthii (formerly Sphaerotheca fuliginea) and Golovinomyces cichoracearum
Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew is the most common foliar disease of squash, pumpkin, melon and cucumber. It reduces photosynthesis, causes early leaf death and lowers fruit quality.
symptoms: White, powdery spots on upper and lower leaf surfaces and on stems; spots enlarge and merge until leaves look dusted with flour
Older leaves are affected first; infected leaves yellow, then turn brown and dry up
Fruit are rarely infected directly but ripen poorly and may sunburn when leaves die
environmental_factors: Warm, dry days with humid nights; the fungus does not need free water on the leaf
Dense canopies and shade
Late-season plantings and high nitrogen
prevention: Grow cultivars with powdery mildew resistance or tolerance
Space plants well and avoid shade to keep humidity down
Scout older leaves weekly from mid-season; protectant and systemic fungicides are widely used but resistance management is important—follow extension guidance
next_steps: Check the undersides of older leaves, where it often starts
Consult extension for resistant cultivars and locally effective products

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: Leaf scorch is a common fungal leaf disease of strawberry. Severe infections weaken plants, reduce yields and increase winter injury.
symptoms: Many small, irregular purple to dark-red spots on the upper leaf surface, without the pale centres seen in common leaf spot
Spots enlarge and merge; the leaf turns purple-brown and dries, looking scorched, and may curl at the edges
Petioles, runners and fruit stalks can also show lesions
environmental_factors: Warm, wet weather; spores are splashed by rain and overhead irrigation
The fungus overwinters on old infected leaves
Dense, weedy or matted beds that dry slowly
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant cultivars
Renovate beds after harvest and remove old leaves
Keep rows narrow, control weeds and avoid overhead irrigation
Fungicides are used in commercial production during the growing season; follow local recommendations
next_steps: Distinguish from common leaf spot (which has grey or white centres) and leaf blight (large V-shaped lesions)

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.scientific_name: Xanthomonas euvesicatoria, X. vesicatoria, X. perforans, X. gardneri
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot causes leaf, stem and fruit lesions on tomato. It is introduced on seed or transplants and spreads rapidly by splashing water in warm, wet weather.
symptoms: Small (under 3 mm), dark, water-soaked spots that may look greasy and often have a yellow halo
Spots can be angular; centres may dry and tear out; heavily spotted leaves yellow and drop
Fruit: small raised, scabby, brown spots
environmental_factors: Warm (24-30 °C), wet conditions and overhead irrigation
Infected seed, transplants and crop debris
Handling wet plants spreads bacteria along rows
prevention: Buy certified disease-free seed and transplants
Rotate away from tomato and pepper and destroy crop residue
Use drip irrigation, mulch and stake plants; avoid working in wet foliage
Copper-based protectants are used but resistance is common; ask extension for current advice
next_steps: Look for raised fruit spots and compare with bacterial speck (smaller spots) and Septoria (spots with light centres)
Lab confirmation is useful because management differs between bacterial and fungal spots

Tomato___Early_blight.scientific_name: Alternaria linariae (A. tomatophila) and A. solani
Tomato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is one of the most common tomato diseases. It causes target-like leaf spots, stem lesions and fruit rot near the stem end, and is worst on stressed or heavily fruiting plants.
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings ('target' pattern) and a yellow halo, starting on the oldest leaves
Lower leaves yellow, wither and drop, progressing up the plant
Dark, sunken lesions on stems and at the stem end of fruit
environmental_factors: Warm, humid weather with alternating wet and dry periods
The fungus survives in soil and debris and on related weeds
Plants stressed by poor nutrition, drought or heavy fruit load
prevention: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops and remove debris
Mulch, stake or cage plants and remove lower infected leaves early
Water at the base; avoid wetting foliage
Resistant or tolerant cultivars and protectant fungicides are available; follow local guidance
next_steps: Remove and bag the worst-affected lower leaves
Monitor weekly; consult extension if the disease moves above the lower third of the plant

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Late blight can kill tomato plants within days in cool, wet weather and spreads to neighbouring gardens and farms. It is considered a community disease.
symptoms: Large, irregular, greasy-looking grey-green to brown lesions on leaves, often starting at the edges
White, fuzzy growth on the underside of lesions in humid weather
Dark brown lesions on stems and firm, brown, greasy blotches on green or ripe fruit

Spores blow in from infected potato or tomato crops; infected transplants and potato cull piles are sources
Overhead irrigation and dense foliage
prevention: Use resistant cultivars where available and buy healthy transplants
Space and stake plants; avoid overhead watering
Follow regional late blight alerts; protectant fungicides are the main commercial tool
Remove and bag infected plants immediately in gardens

Tell nearby growers if confirmed; do not compost infected material

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.scientific_name: Passalora fulva (syn. Fulvia fulva, Cladosporium fulvum)
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Leaf mold is primarily a disease of greenhouse and high-tunnel tomatoes, where humidity stays high. It rarely matters in dry, well-ventilated conditions.
symptoms: Pale green or yellowish spots on the upper leaf surface with indistinct edges
Olive-green to brown, velvety mould on the corresponding underside
Leaves yellow, curl and drop, starting with the oldest

Poor ventilation in greenhouses and tunnels; mild temperatures
The fungus survives on debris and as spores on structures
prevention: Ventilate and heat to keep humidity down; space plants and prune lower leaves
Water early in the day at the base of plants
Grow cultivars with leaf mold resistance (Cf genes), noting that resistance can be overcome by new races
Sanitise the structure between crops
next_steps: Check leaf undersides for velvety mould to confirm
Improve ventilation immediately; consult extension for resistant cultivars

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot is a very common foliar disease that defoliates tomato plants from the bottom up, exposing fruit to sunscald and reducing yield.

Tiny black dots (pycnidia) visible in the centre of older spots with a hand lens
Starts on lower leaves after the first fruit set; leaves yellow, brown and drop

Infected debris, volunteer tomatoes and solanaceous weeds
Overhead irrigation and crowded plantings
prevention: Rotate for 2-3 years and remove crop debris

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Two-spotted spider mites are tiny arachnids that feed on leaf cells. Damage looks like a disease but is caused by thousands of feeding punctures; hot, dry weather and some insecticides make outbreaks worse.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling (speckles) on the upper leaf surface
Leaves turn bronze or yellow and dry out; fine webbing on the undersides and between leaves in heavy infestations
Tiny moving dots (mites) visible on the underside with a hand lens
environmental_factors: Hot, dry, dusty conditions
Water-stressed plants
Use of broad-spectrum insecticides that kill the mites' natural enemies
prevention: Keep plants well watered and reduce dust
Conserve natural enemies (predatory mites, lady beetles); avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticides
Spraying leaf undersides with water can suppress light infestations
Horticultural oils, soaps and miticides are options; rotate modes of action and follow labels

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Target spot is a fungal disease of tomato foliage and fruit that is most important in warm, humid production regions. It is easily confused with early blight.
symptoms: Small brown lesions that enlarge into spots with concentric rings and a yellow margin on leaves
Spots can appear throughout the canopy rather than only on lower leaves

Dense canopies; the fungus has a very wide host range including weeds and other crops
Survives on crop debris
prevention: Rotate and remove debris; control weeds that can host the fungus
Space and stake plants for airflow; avoid overhead irrigation
Protectant fungicides are used commercially; follow regional guidance

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: TYLCV is transmitted by the silverleaf/sweetpotato whitefly. Plants infected young are severely stunted and produce little or no fruit. There is no cure once a plant is infected.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: ToMV is an extremely stable virus spread on hands, tools and seed rather than by insects. It is closely related to tobacco mosaic virus and survives for long periods in debris and on surfaces.
